title: Server timeouts, graceful shutdown, static files with embed
summary: The zero http.Server has no timeouts, so one slow client can hold a connection forever: set them. Shut down with Server.Shutdown, which drains requests but cancels none, and ship static assets inside the binary with embed and FileServerFS.

examples.title: What ReadHeaderTimeout and WriteTimeout do, and what the client sees

annotations.note: The slowloris attack in miniature: valid but unfinished headers, sent by a client that then just waits. Each such connection pins a goroutine and a file descriptor; a few thousand of them exhaust a server without sending much traffic.
errors.AsType (Go 1.26) finds the net.Error and returns it typed. A read deadline that passes is a timeout; anything else here means the server hung up.
httptest.NewServer, like http.ListenAndServe, uses a zero http.Server: every timeout is zero, which means none. That is the dangerous default this lesson is about.
NewUnstartedServer exposes the *http.Server as Config, so a test can set fields before Start. ReadHeaderTimeout closes the connection without any response, not even a 408.

WriteTimeout is not a request timeout with a polite answer: when it passes, the client gets a closed connection and no status at all, while the handler's write succeeded into a buffer and it never learned. Use it as a backstop, and per-request deadlines (previous lesson) for answers.

examples.title: Shutdown drains in-flight requests; long-lived ones need a signal

annotations.note: Listening on 127.0.0.1:0 lets the OS choose a free port; the listener knows which. Binding to 127.0.0.1 rather than ":8080" keeps a development server off the network.
Shutdown does not cancel request contexts and does not wait for hijacked connections such as WebSockets. A context canceled from RegisterOnShutdown gives streams and long polls their stop signal.

BaseContext is the root of every request's context on this server, so canceling it reaches every handler at once. RegisterOnShutdown functions run in their own goroutines when Shutdown starts; they should start the goodbye, not wait for it.

Always give Shutdown a deadline. Without one, a single stuck request blocks the process forever; with one, Shutdown returns the context's error and you can call srv.Close() to cut the remaining connections.
Serve returns http.ErrServerClosed immediately, while two requests are still running. A main that returns at that moment kills them mid-response: main must wait for Shutdown, not for Serve.
The stream ended because RegisterOnShutdown canceled its context. The report finished its work and got its 200: drained, not dropped. Only then did Shutdown return nil.

examples.title: Serving embedded files with fs.Sub and http.FileServerFS

annotations.note: //go:embed is read at compile time: the files must sit next to the source, and the build fails if they are missing. Embedding a directory skips names starting with "." or "_" (_draft.html below); the "all:static" pattern would include them.

Forgetting fs.Sub is the classic bug: every URL then needs a /static/ segment, or nothing matches. StackLab's backend hit the same trap with its embedded migrations; main.go's migrationsFS exists for it.
FileServerFS (Go 1.22) takes any fs.FS: embed.FS, os.DirFS, or a testing/fstest.MapFS in tests. StripPrefix removes /assets/ so the remaining path matches names inside the FS.

Content-Type comes from the extension. Last-Modified is empty because embedded files have a zero ModTime, so browsers can't revalidate with If-Modified-Since. index.html redirects to its directory, and a directory without an index gets a listing.

use_cases: Any production http.Server: ReadHeaderTimeout always, the others according to the slowest legitimate request
Rolling deploys and container restarts: SIGTERM, stop accepting, drain, exit before the orchestrator's kill deadline
Single-binary tools and admin UIs that carry their HTML, CSS and JavaScript (or a built React app) inside the executable
Embedding SQL migrations or templates so a distroless image needs nothing but the binary
strengths: Shutdown is built in and correct by default (stop accepting, close idle, wait for active), where many stacks need a library or careful signal handling
Per-route exceptions without a second server: http.ResponseController.SetWriteDeadline extends one handler's deadline
embed.FS is an fs.FS, so the same code serves embedded files in production and os.DirFS or fstest.MapFS in development and tests
One static binary with its assets: no working-directory surprises, unlike Java resources resolved at run time or Node's static folders
weaknesses: Safe timeouts are opt-in: http.ListenAndServe and the zero http.Server have none, unlike Node's 60 s headersTimeout and 300 s requestTimeout (since Node 18)
Server-wide ReadTimeout and WriteTimeout can't tell a slow upload or a stream from an attack; long routes need per-request handling
Shutdown neither cancels handlers nor tracks WebSockets; long-lived work needs BaseContext or RegisterOnShutdown wiring
Embedded files have no modification time, so FileServerFS sends no Last-Modified; caching needs ETags or fingerprinted file names

pitfalls.title: http.ListenAndServe in production
pitfalls.detail: It uses a zero http.Server, so there is no way to set timeouts. Build an http.Server and set at least ReadHeaderTimeout.
pitfalls.good:
srv := &http.Server{Addr: "127.0.0.1:8080", Handler: mux,
	ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second, IdleTimeout: time.Minute}

pitfalls.title: Exiting when ListenAndServe returns
pitfalls.detail: After Shutdown starts, ListenAndServe returns http.ErrServerClosed at once. If main returns there, in-flight requests die. Wait for Shutdown to return.

pitfalls.title: Treating ErrServerClosed as a failure
pitfalls.detail: It is the expected result after Shutdown or Close. Check errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) before logging an error or exiting non-zero.

pitfalls.title: A global WriteTimeout shorter than your slowest route
pitfalls.detail: The client of a long export or SSE stream gets a dropped connection, and the handler's writes may look successful. Extend the deadline for that route with http.NewResponseController(w).SetWriteDeadline, which needs Unwrap on any wrapping middleware.

pitfalls.title: Expecting dotfiles and _files in an embedded directory
pitfalls.detail: //go:embed static skips names starting with . or _. Frameworks that emit _app.js or similar need //go:embed all:static.

quiz.q: What are the timeouts of a server started with http.ListenAndServe(addr, mux)?
options: None: every timeout is zero, meaning no deadline
quiz.why: ListenAndServe builds a zero http.Server, and a zero timeout means no timeout. Set them on your own http.Server.

quiz.q: A handler takes longer than the server's WriteTimeout. What does the client see?
options: The connection closes without a response
quiz.why: The write deadline expires on the connection; the buffered response can't be sent and the connection is closed. No status line reaches the client.

quiz.q: Shutdown(ctx) is called while an SSE handler waits on r.Context().Done(). Without further wiring, what happens?
options: The handler's context is canceled at once
Shutdown waits for the handler until ctx expires
quiz.why: Shutdown waits for active connections but cancels nothing. Cancel a BaseContext from RegisterOnShutdown to end such handlers.

quiz.q: Why does FileServerFS over an embed.FS send no Last-Modified header?
options: Embedded files have a zero modification time, and ServeContent omits a zero time
quiz.why: embed.FS reports a zero ModTime; ServeContent only sets Last-Modified for a non-zero time. Use an ETag or fingerprinted names for caching.

body:
## Concept

An `http.Server` is configuration plus a loop that accepts connections. Its zero value,
which `http.ListenAndServe` uses, has **no timeouts**: a client that sends headers slowly,
never finishes a body, or never reads the response holds a goroutine and a socket for as
long as it likes. Four fields bound the phases of a connection:

| Field | Bounds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `ReadHeaderTimeout` | reading the request line and headers | set it always; the slowloris defense |
| `ReadTimeout` | reading the whole request, body included | blunt for uploads; often left to per-request limits |
| `WriteTimeout` | from the end of the headers to the end of the response | effectively caps handler time; the client gets no response when it fires |
| `IdleTimeout` | waiting for the next request on a keep-alive connection | falls back to `ReadTimeout` when zero |

Header size has a limit by default: `MaxHeaderBytes` defaults to 1 MB, and Go 1.27 added
`MaxHeaderValueCount` (default 500 values). One route can relax the server-wide deadlines
with `http.NewResponseController(w).SetWriteDeadline(...)` (Go 1.20).

**Graceful shutdown** is `srv.Shutdown(ctx)`: close the listeners, close idle connections,
wait for active requests to finish. `Serve` returns `http.ErrServerClosed` as soon as it
starts, so `main` must wait for `Shutdown` to return. Shutdown never cancels a request's
context and ignores hijacked connections, so streams and WebSockets need their own signal.

**Static files** can live in the binary: `//go:embed static` fills an `embed.FS` at compile
time, `fs.Sub` drops the directory prefix, and `http.FileServerFS` (Go 1.22) serves it with
content types, range requests and conditional GETs.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Node**: `http.createServer` has defaults: `headersTimeout` 60 s and, since Node 18,
  `requestTimeout` 300 s. Go starts at zero, and you choose. Draining on SIGTERM is your
  code in both: `process.on('SIGTERM', ...)` there, `signal.NotifyContext` here.
- **Java**: a servlet container ships preconfigured connection timeouts and its own
  graceful-shutdown setting. In Go the server is a struct in your `main`, and so is its
  lifecycle.
- **Python**: gunicorn or uvicorn own the timeouts and the SIGTERM handling outside your
  code. In Go there is no separate application server: your binary is it.
- **C/C++**: `go:embed` is what `xxd -i` or C23's `#embed` do for a byte array, but it
  produces a read-only file system with directories, not one blob.

## Design notes

StackLab's `cmd/stacklab/main.go` is a complete lifecycle to read: `ReadHeaderTimeout` 5 s,
`ReadTimeout` and `WriteTimeout` from configuration (15 s), `IdleTimeout` 60 s;
`signal.NotifyContext` for Ctrl+C and SIGTERM; `ListenAndServe` in a goroutine, ignoring
`ErrServerClosed`; and `Shutdown` with a 10 s budget. The run route is the one exception
to the 15 s write deadline: it extends its own deadline with `ResponseController`, because
a lesson run may take longer.

Pick the drain budget from the slowest request you are willing to wait for, and keep it
below the time your process manager waits before killing the process. If `Shutdown` returns
`context.DeadlineExceeded`, call `srv.Close()`, log, and exit. For a service behind a load
balancer, fail the readiness check first (StackLab has `/readyz`), so traffic stops arriving
before the listener closes.

For embedded assets, decide on caching explicitly. With content-hashed file names, as a
Vite build emits, serve them with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. For
fixed names, compute a hash per file at startup and set it as the `ETag` header before
calling the file server; `ServeContent` then answers `If-None-Match` with 304. A single-page
app also needs a fallback that serves `index.html` for unknown paths outside `/api/` and
`/assets/`.

files.examples/02_graceful_shutdown.go:
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net"
	"net/http"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0") // port 0: the OS picks a free one
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	base := "http://" + ln.Addr().String()

	// Shutdown waits for requests but never cancels them. Long-lived ones
	// (streams, long polls) need a signal: this context, canceled on Shutdown.
	serverCtx, stopStreams := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
	started, release := make(chan bool, 2), make(chan bool)
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /report", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		started <- true
		<-release // slow work in progress
		io.WriteString(w, "report done")
	})
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /events", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		started <- true
		<-r.Context().Done() // a stream ends when the client or the server does
		io.WriteString(w, "stream closed: server shutting down")
	})
	srv := &http.Server{
		Handler:           mux,
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
		BaseContext:       func(net.Listener) context.Context { return serverCtx },
	}
	srv.RegisterOnShutdown(stopStreams)
	served := make(chan error, 1)
	go func() { served <- srv.Serve(ln) }()

	get := func(path string) <-chan string {
		out := make(chan string, 1)
		go func() {
			resp, err := http.Get(base + path)
			if err != nil {
				out <- path + ": no response"
				return
			}
			defer resp.Body.Close()
			body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
			out <- fmt.Sprintf("%s: %d %s", path, resp.StatusCode, body)
		}()
		return out
	}
	report, events := get("/report"), get("/events")
	<-started
	<-started // both requests are in flight

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	shutdown := make(chan error, 1)
	go func() { shutdown <- srv.Shutdown(ctx) }()

	fmt.Println("Serve returned:", <-served)
	_, err = net.Dial("tcp", ln.Addr().String())
	fmt.Println("new connections refused:", err != nil)
	fmt.Println(<-events)
	close(release)
	fmt.Println(<-report)
	fmt.Println("Shutdown returned:", <-shutdown)
}
